strengths: Does not treat tabearuki as illegal; “nobody is issuing tickets” is the right legal temperature.
Festivals, ice cream, drinks, theme parks, and snack streets are named as ordinary exceptions.
FAQ explicitly rejects “Japanese people never eat outdoors.”
Bin scarcity is framed as reinforcing inconvenience, not as the sole cause of the manners pattern—correctly split from the trash-can sibling article.
Rejects the unique-discipline / unique-cleanliness travel-writing myth.

issues.location: ## How Japanese People Learn the Pause — outdoor eating as a “special case”
issues.problem: Overstates Japanese meal norms. Outdoor eating is widespread; what is uncommon on weekday sidewalks is combining eating with walking through other people’s path. The line also contradicts the FAQ.
issues.suggestion: Replace the two-step “special case / second special case” ladder with: seated meals at home are typical; outdoor eating happens often; walking-eating on a commuter sidewalk is the extra, crowded-space layer.

issues.location: ## When Eating on the Move Is Ordinary — tourist neighborhoods
issues.problem: The snack-economy hedge is mostly right, but a visitor can still map “tourist and crowded” onto historic approaches where walking-eating is asked against, not invited.
issues.suggestion: One contrast: handheld-snack streets versus sightseeing streets that stay crowded but still treat tabearuki as a nuisance. Do not invent a municipal ban.

issues.problem: Desk kyushoku and classroom cleaning are real in many elementary schools, but they are presented as a clean causal pipeline into adult sidewalk manners.
issues.suggestion: Keep as one training thread among others, not as the origin story.
